subject: Collision Avoidance
learning_objective: State when most midair collision accidents occur.
question_text: Most midair collision accidents occur during

choices.label: A
choices.text: hazy days within the traffic pattern environment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: clear days in the vicinity of navigational aids.

choices.label: C
choices.text: night conditions during simulated instrument flight.

explanation: Most midair collisions occur in good (clear) visibility conditions, often near navigational aids or airports where traffic converges — good weather can paradoxically reduce vigilance since pilots may assume 'see and avoid' is straightforward.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Haze reduces visual detection range and contributes to some collisions, but statistically most midairs occur in clear conditions.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Simulated instrument flight is a controlled training scenario with a safety pilot and is not the most common midair collision circumstance.

subject: Human Factors - Night Vision
learning_objective: State the effective technique for detecting other aircraft at night.
question_text: The most effective technique to use for detecting other aircraft at night is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: turn the head and sweep the eyes rapidly over the entire visible region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: avoid staring directly at the point where another aircraft is suspected to be flying.

choices.label: C
choices.text: avoid scanning the region below the horizon so as to avoid the effect of ground lights on the eyes.

explanation: At night, off-center (peripheral) viewing is more effective than direct fixation, because the eye's more light-sensitive rod cells are concentrated outside the central fovea; looking slightly to the side of a suspected target often reveals it better than staring directly at it.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Rapid sweeping reduces the eyes' ability to detect faint targets, which requires a brief pause to allow the rods to register dim light.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The region below the horizon should not be categorically excluded from scanning; the key technique is off-center viewing, not avoiding certain sky regions.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), night vision.
source_title: FIA - Flight Instructor Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Airport Operations - Non-Towered Departure
learning_objective: State the correct departure procedure at a non-towered airport.
question_text: What is the correct departure procedure at a non-towered airport?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The FAA-approved departure procedure for that airport.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Make all left turns, except a 45° right turn on the first crosswind leg.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Departure in any direction consistent with safety, after crossing the airport boundary.

explanation: At a non-towered airport, once clear of the traffic pattern (after crossing the airport boundary), a pilot may depart in any direction consistent with safety, subject to any published noise abatement or local procedures.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: There is no universal 'FAA-approved departure procedure' requirement for every non-towered airport.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This describes a specific, non-standard local procedure, not the general default rule.

regulation_reference: AIM, traffic pattern operations at airports without an operating control tower.

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Regulations - Carriage of Intoxicated Persons
learning_objective: State the exception permitting carriage of an intoxicated person aboard an aircraft.
question_text: Under what condition, if any, may a pilot allow a person who is obviously under the influence of intoxicating liquors or drugs to be carried aboard an aircraft?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only if a second pilot is aboard.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only if the person is a medical patient under proper care or in an emergency.

explanation: 14 CFR 91.17(b) permits carrying a person who appears intoxicated only if that person is a medical patient under proper care, or in an emergency.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: There is a narrow regulatory exception, so 'under no condition' overstates the rule.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Having a second pilot aboard is not the regulatory basis for this exception.

subject: Regulations - Parachute Requirements
learning_objective: State when occupants must wear an approved parachute.
question_text: When must each occupant of an aircraft wear an approved parachute?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When flying over water beyond gliding distance to the shore.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When practicing spins or other flight maneuvers for any certificate or rating.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When an intentional maneuver that exceeds 30° noseup or nosedown relative to the horizon is made.

explanation: 14 CFR 91.307 requires each occupant to wear an approved parachute when an intentional maneuver exceeds a nose-up or nose-down pitch attitude of 30 degrees relative to the horizon (or a bank of more than 60 degrees), subject to specified training/flight-test exceptions.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Flying beyond gliding distance to shore relates to life preserver/raft requirements, not parachute requirements.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Spin/maneuver training for a certificate or rating given by an authorized instructor is specifically exempted from the parachute requirement under 91.307(c).

subject: Regulations - Annual Inspection
learning_objective: Calculate the next annual inspection due date.
question_text: An aircraft's last annual inspection was performed on July 12, this year. The next annual inspection will be due no later than

choices.label: C
choices.text: 12 calendar months after the date shown on the Airworthiness Certificate.

explanation: Annual inspections are due within 12 calendar months of the previous annual inspection, which runs to the end of the 12th month following the month of the last inspection — so an inspection performed in July is due again by the end of July the following year.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Using the exact anniversary date rather than the 'end of the 12th calendar month' rule understates the allowed window.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The due date is based on the previous annual inspection date, not the date shown on the Airworthiness Certificate.

calculation_steps: 12 calendar months from July (this year) = due by the end of July (next year).

subject: Regulations - ELT Inspection

question_text: How often are emergency locator transmitters required to be inspected?

choices.label: C

explanation: ELTs must be inspected within the preceding 12 calendar months (14 CFR 91.207(d)) — distinct from the 24-calendar-month interval required for transponder tests.

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: ELT inspection is calendar-based (12 months), not tied to a flight-hour interval.

subject: Regulations - Night-Unequipped Aircraft
learning_objective: Calculate the latest time a night-unequipped aircraft may be operated relative to sunset.
question_text: If an aircraft is not equipped for night flight and official sunset is 1730 EST, the latest a pilot may operate that aircraft without violating regulations is
explanation: Because position lights (which a night-unequipped aircraft lacks) are required from sunset onward, an aircraft not equipped for night flight must be on the ground, or its flight otherwise concluded, by sunset — effectively the latest permissible operating time is just before 1730, i.e. 1729 EST.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 1629 EST (one hour before sunset) is more restrictive than the actual regulatory cutoff of sunset itself.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 1829 EST (one hour after sunset) would violate the position-light requirement, which begins exactly at sunset.

calculation_steps: Position lights are required from sunset (1730 EST). A night-unequipped aircraft must therefore cease operating no later than immediately before sunset, i.e. 1729 EST.

subject: Aerodynamics - V-Speeds
learning_objective: Define V2 speed.
question_text: What is V2 speed?
explanation: V2 is the takeoff safety speed — the minimum speed at which the required climb performance can be achieved after an engine failure at or after V1, for transport-category-type operations.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Takeoff decision speed is V1, not V2.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 'Minimum takeoff speed' is not the specific defined term for V2.

explanation: 'SLGT' (Slight Risk) is the Convective Outlook category used when well-organized severe thunderstorms are expected but in small numbers and/or with low coverage.

subject: Weather - In-Flight Advisories
learning_objective: Identify the in-flight advisory containing information on severe icing.
question_text: Which in-flight advisory would contain information on severe icing?
explanation: A SIGMET (Significant Meteorological Information) advisory covers hazards including severe icing, severe turbulence, dust/sandstorms, and volcanic ash, and is issued for all aircraft.

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A Convective SIGMET is specifically for thunderstorm-related hazards (embedded thunderstorms, lines of thunderstorms, hail), not general severe icing.

subject: Weather - Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast
learning_objective: Decode a winds and temperatures aloft forecast (FB) entry.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-5H, Figure 7.) What wind is forecast for STL at 9,000 feet?
explanation: The STL row at the 9,000 ft column reads '2332+02': the first two digits (23) give wind direction in tens of degrees (230°), the next two digits (32) give wind speed in knots, and '+02' gives temperature in degrees Celsius. Winds aloft forecasts are always reported relative to true north.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 25 knots misreads the speed group; the forecast shows 32 knots.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Winds and temperatures aloft forecasts are given relative to true, not magnetic, north.

handbook_reference: FAA-CT-8080-5H, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement, Figure 7 (Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast).
calculation_steps: STL column at 9,000 ft = '2332+02'. Direction = 23 x 10 = 230 degrees true. Speed = 32 knots. Temperature = +02 degC.

subject: Aerodynamics - V-n (Velocity/Load Factor) Diagram
learning_objective: Identify the airspeed represented by a labelled point on a V-n diagram.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-5H, Figure 17.) The airspeed indicated by point A is
explanation: Point A is at the bottom of the V-n (velocity/load factor) envelope, at 1G and the lowest airspeed on the curve — explicitly labelled 'Normal stall speed' on the chart.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Maneuvering speed is at the corner where the stall line meets the positive load limit line (point B on this chart), not point A.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Maximum structural cruising speed is at the upper boundary of the green 'normal operating range' (point D on this chart), not point A.

regulation_reference: Standard V-n diagram / structural limitations theory.

subject: Aerodynamics - Accelerated Stall Speed
learning_objective: Calculate accelerated stall speed at a given load factor using the stall-speed-vs-load-factor relationship.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-5H, Figure 18.) What is the stall speed of an airplane under a load factor of 2 if the unaccelerated stall speed is 100 knots?
explanation: Accelerated stall speed equals the unaccelerated stall speed multiplied by the square root of the load factor. At a load factor of 2, this gives approximately a 41% increase in stall speed, consistent with the Stall Speed vs. Load Factor chart's curve at the bank angle corresponding to a load factor of 2 (60 degrees).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 115 knots corresponds to a smaller percentage increase than the actual ~41% increase at a load factor of 2.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 129 knots understates the calculated/charted increase for a load factor of 2.

handbook_reference: FAA-CT-8080-5H, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement, Figure 18 (Stall Speed vs. Load Factor).
calculation_steps: Accelerated stall speed = unaccelerated stall speed x sqrt(load factor) = 100 x sqrt(2) = 100 x 1.414 = 141.4 knots, closest to 140 knots.
source_title: FIA - Flight Instructor Airplane sample questions

subject: Navigation - Crosswind Component
learning_objective: Calculate the crosswind component for a landing given runway heading and reported wind.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-5H, Figure 30.) What is the crosswind component for a landing on Runway 18 if the tower reports the wind as 220° at 25 knots?
explanation: Runway 18 has a magnetic heading of 180°. The wind is from 220°, giving a 40° angle between the wind and the runway. Reading the Wind Component Chart (or computing trigonometrically) at 25 knots and 40° gives a crosswind component of approximately 16 knots.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 19 knots is the headwind component for this scenario (25 x cos 40°), not the crosswind component.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 22 knots does not match either the crosswind or headwind component for this scenario.

handbook_reference: FAA-CT-8080-5H, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement, Figure 30 (Wind Component Chart).
calculation_steps: Runway 18 heading = 180 degrees. Angle off runway = 220 - 180 = 40 degrees. Crosswind component = 25 x sin(40 deg) = 25 x 0.643 = 16.1 knots, approximately 16 knots. (Headwind component = 25 x cos(40 deg) = 19.2 knots, the distractor in option B.)
source_title: FIA - Flight Instructor Airplane sample questions
